docs.description: Bastiat, Frédéric. The Law . Translated by Dennis O'Keeffe, revised by David M. Hart, Liberty Fund, 2018. Originally published 1850. AP/IB Student Analysis of The Law by Frédéric Bastiat (1850) 1. Historical and Political Context Bastiat wrote The Law in June 1850 amid the political upheaval following the 1848 French Revolution and during the short-lived Second Republic. France was grappling with socialism, class struggle, the expansion of suffrage, and debates about the proper role of government. Bastiat, a classical liberal and member of the National Assembly, responded to what he saw as a perversion of the law—especially socialism and protectionism—by articulating a defense of individual liberty and property. 2. Legal Philosophy and Foundations Bastiat grounds his legal theory in natural law . He argues that life, liberty, and property are pre-political, God-given rights that precede the state. Law, therefore, should exist only to protect these rights. He opposes positive law when it contradicts natural law—particularly when laws are used to redistribute property unjustly or support state-sanctioned "legal plunder." 3. Moral Framework and Justice Justice for Bastiat is synonymous with non-aggression: the law must never violate the rights it is meant to protect. Ethical values emphasized include freedom , non-coercion , individual responsibility , and justice through limitation . He critiques socialism and redistribution as fundamentally immoral because they reward theft under the guise of legality. 4. Faith, Religion, and the Law Bastiat makes frequent reference to God and Providence , asserting that life and the rights of liberty and property are divine gifts. Although he does not promote a theocratic state, he presents law as a moral force derived from divine and natural principles. His invocation of God is rhetorical and philosophical, supporting a deistic rather than ecclesiastical vision. 5. Purpose and Function of Legal Institutions Legal institutions are tools for collective self-defense , not engines of social engineering. Bastiat argues that courts and legislatures should only defend life, liberty, and property. When law becomes a tool for redistribution or social planning, it transforms from protector to oppressor—violating its moral function. 6. Epistemology: Knowledge, Law, and Truth Bastiat believes that knowledge of law and justice arises through reason and moral instinct , rather than legislation alone. He critiques those who see the legislator as a superior being guiding inferior citizens. Lawmakers must recognize they are subject to the same natural rights as all. 7. Civic Virtue and the Role of the Citizen Citizens are portrayed as rational and moral agents with the duty to defend liberty. Bastiat insists that they should neither expect the state to provide for them nor use the law for personal gain. Ideal lawmakers and jurors uphold justice by resisting the temptation of "legal plunder" and respecting the limits of state power. 8. Rhetorical Style and Argumentation Bastiat’s writing blends deductive logic , historical analogy , and satirical critique . He uses striking antitheses (e.g., law as protector vs. law as plunderer) and rhetorical questions to force readers to confront contradictions in legal reasoning. His tone is moralistic but persuasive, appealing to both conscience and logic. 9. Implicit Assumptions and Biases Bastiat assumes a universal applicability of natural rights and that free markets and minimal government are the default moral and political order. He is deeply skeptical of state power and assumes a high degree of civic rationality and virtue. The poor are seen as potentially manipulated rather than naturally dependent. 10. Modern Relevance and Application Bastiat’s critique of "legal plunder" resonates in contemporary debates over welfare states, redistributive taxation, tariffs, and socialism . His insights align with libertarian critiques of modern governments and inform discussions on civil liberties, constitutional limits , and economic justice . His analysis also parallels arguments against populist and corporatist corruption of law. Suggested Student Discussion Questions Natural vs. Positive Law : What does Bastiat mean when he says that property exists before law? How does this challenge modern legal systems? Justice and Redistribution : According to Bastiat, when does law become injustice? How would he respond to welfare programs or progressive taxation? Religion and Rights : What is the role of divine authority in Bastiat’s concept of law? Is his argument theologically grounded or morally philosophical? Legal Plunder : How does Bastiat distinguish between legal and illegal plunder? Can you identify modern examples of each? Citizenship and Civic Responsibility : What does Bastiat expect from citizens in a just society? How does this compare with civic expectations in today’s democracies?

docs.creator: Tracy Rosenthal
docs.description: Both a forceful polemic and a practical guide, Abolish Rent takes aim at one of the foremost engines of inequality and injustice. Rent is a wealth transfer from the poorest to the richest, the most vulnerable to the least, a monthly tribute that drives millions to debt, despair, and into the streets. In the context of a permanent housing crisis and governments in the pocket of real estate interests, Abolish Rent reorients the politics of housing around tenants political actors who can, through organizing, direct action, and collective bargaining, bring about a housing system that meets their needs.  Abolish Rent is the first book-length engagement with the resurgent tenant movement. Authors Tracy Rosenthal and Leonardo Vilchis—cofounders of Los Angles’s many thousand member tenant union—offer a deeply-reported account centering poor and working class tenants who are fighting back, staying put, and remaking the city in the process. They take us to trilingual strategy meetings, raucous marches against gentrification, and daring eviction defenses where immigrants put their lives on the line.  If rent abolition is our aim, tenant power must be the means—built through everyday resistance in our buildings and on our blocks. This is the revolutionary project we need to make our housing, our cities, and the world our home.
docs.title: Abolish Rent: How Tenants Can Solve The Housing Crisis

"A book about contemporary political culture in Washington, DC"--

Washington funerals can make great networking opportunities. Disgraced Hill aides can overcome ignominy and emerge with a more potent "brand" than many elected members of Congress. There are no Democrats and Republicans anymore in the nation's capital, just millionaires. That is the grubby secret of the place in the twenty-first century: no matter how many elections you lose, apologies you make, or scandals you endure, Washington is the nexus of big politics, big money, big media, and big vanity
docs.title: This town : two parties and a funeral--plus, plenty of valet parking!--in America's gilded capital
